Source: https://theaiengineer.substack.com/p/what-is-agentic-search
Title: What Is Agentic Search? A Model Searching in a Loop
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Agentic search is a model searching in a loop: it writes a query, reads the results and picks its next move, whether that is another search, a page to open or the answer. For example, a coding agent uses it to find the code behind a bug, and a research agent to gather sources for a report. It costs more than one search, and it often pays off when the first search misses.
You run this loop yourself whenever a first search fails. You type an error message into a search box and skim the results. The page you need is missing, so you rewrite the query from what you just read, open the page that looks closest and answer once you have it. Each step uses what the step before it found.
Hand that loop to a model and you have agentic search. The model writes the query, reads the results and picks the next move. Each call to the model carries only what its request holds, so your code sends the question and every result so far with every call. Re-sending is often where the loop's cost comes from.
Real questions often need facts from several pages. The 2022 Self-Ask paper uses the smallest case, 2 facts from 2 pages: who was president of the United States when superconductivity was discovered? In the paper's figure, GPT-3 answered it with no search at all and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt. That answer is wrong, and one search does no better.
The loop splits the question. Its first search asks when superconductivity was discovered and finds 1911. Its second search, written from that answer, asks who was president in 1911 and finds William Howard Taft.
One search answers from whatever its top result proposes, and the loop writes its second search from what the first one found.
The paper's authors then wrote Bamboogle, 125 questions of this 2-step kind. In the paper's test, Google answered 0.0% of them right from the question as typed. With GPT-3 writing its own follow-up searches, the paper measured 60.0%.1

One search is how **RAG** works in its basic form. Retrieval-augmented generation sends the user's words to a search, puts the top results in the prompt and lets the model answer from them. Ask RAG the superconductivity question, and it answers from whatever ranked first. In agentic search, the model can reject those results and search again.
> 🔗 Retrieval by meaning over your own documents is the subject of **What is Semantic Search?**
> 🔗 Other ways to put a model in the retrieval loop are compared in **Agentic RAG vs CUA vs A2A**
When you build a search agent or debug one that answers wrong, you need to know which part does what. To search, the model writes a request such as `search("Brave Search API price")`: the name of a function your code exposes, and its argument. That request is a tool call. Your code runs the function and sends the result back as the next message.
> 🔗 First time handing a model a function to call? **What is Function Calling?** walks through one call end to end.
Agentic search runs that exchange in a loop, with every decision left to the model: what to search, which page to open and when to answer. The loop has 4 parts:
1.   **The model** writes every query and picks the next move.

2.   **A search tool** sends the query to a search API, which answers from its index: a stored copy of web pages, organized so a query finds the pages that match it.

3.   **A fetch tool** downloads one page the model asks to read in full.

4.   **Your code** starts the run, runs each tool call, sends the result back and stops the run at a cap of 8 model calls.
Your code sends the question and the 2 tools, then runs every tool call and re-sends the whole conversation, until the model answers or your code stops it at 8 calls.
> 🔗 Agents in general? **What is an AI Agent?** covers the loop in which the model decides when to stop.
You choose who does the searching. Build the search and fetch tools yourself, and your code runs every search, so you see each query and set the cap. Or switch on the search a model provider already offers, and its servers do the searching while you write less code.2

You have probably watched this loop without knowing its name. Ask a coding assistant to fix a bug, and it searches your files, reads what it finds and searches again before it answers.
**Coding agents search your code.** Claude Code runs grep and glob, the command-line tools you already use to search file contents and file names, over your repository. Its creator, Boris Cherny, posted in February 2026 that early versions searched a stored index of your files, an approach called RAG. In his words, "we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better." **How Claude Code Actually Works** walks through that search.3
**Deep research usually runs the longest loops.** OpenAI's documentation says its deep research can "find, analyze, and synthesize hundreds of sources", and that a run "can take tens of minutes". Anthropic's own deep research agent is the subject of **How Anthropic Built Multi-Agent Deep Research**.4
**Chat assistants search the web, and ChatGPT moved to the loop in 2026.** David Konitzny measured ChatGPT before and after GPT-5.6 became the default in August 2026. A round is one batch of searches the model sends before it reads any results. In his dataset, 94.0% of prompts got a single round before the change. After the change, 43.5% got one round, and the other 56.5% searched again from what the first round found.5
> ⚠️ **Turning on web search can still mean one search.** OpenAI's documentation describes non-reasoning web search, in which a model that answers without a thinking step sends your question to the search tool and relays the top results.6
A loop that searches again and again can still answer worse than one search. The loop often pays on questions that need more than one page, but only for a model that has learned to run it. The same loop that helps one model can leave another worse off than one search.

BrowseComp-Plus is a 2025 benchmark of hard research questions over a fixed set of documents. Its authors raised gpt-oss-20B's reasoning effort, the budget it spends thinking before it acts. The extra thinking led it to search 23.87 times per question, up from 1.87. The benchmark scored the model's right answers at 34.58%, up from 13.37%.7
Before you rely on the loop, test it on your own questions. Take 2-step questions whose answers you know and run the loop below twice, once allowing 2 model calls and once allowing 8. Count the right answers each time: if 8 calls do not beat 2, the extra calls are only costing you. That test is a small eval, and **What is an Eval?** shows how to build a bigger one. The Search-R1 paper of March 2025 is the warning. On Qwen2.5-7B, a small open model, loops built by prompting alone scored lower than one search, and only the version trained to run the loop beat it.8
On list prices and the token sizes assumed below, a loop of 4 searches costs about 5 times what one search and an answer cost. Models read text, and providers bill it, in tokens, short chunks of a few characters each. Every model call sends the whole conversation again, so the loop pays for each search again on every later call.
Take a run of 4 searches, 1 page fetch and the answer, which is 6 model calls. I assume the prompt starts at 1,500 tokens and each tool call the model writes adds 150. Each search adds 2,064 tokens of results, the size OpenBenchmarks measured for the Brave Search API. The loop below asks for at most 2,064. The fetched page adds about 2,500 more tokens, my assumption for a 10 kB page. That brings the 6th call to 13,006.9
Your code re-sends the first search result on 5 of the 6 calls, so the loop pays for it 5 times.

You run this loop yourself whenever a first search fails. You type an error message into a search box and skim the results. Agentic search is a model searching in a loop: it writes a query, reads the results and picks its next move, whether that is another search, a page to open or the answer. For example, a coding agent uses it to find the code behind a bug, and a research agent to gather sources for a report. It costs more than one search, and it often pays off when the first search misses.
You run this loop yourself whenever a first search fails. You type an error message into a search box and skim the results. The page you need is missing, so you rewrite the query from what you just read, open the page that looks closest and answer once you have it. Each step uses what the step before it found.
Hand that loop to a model and you have agentic search. The model writes the query, reads the results and picks the next move. Each call to the model carries only what its request holds, so your code sends the question and every result so far with every call. Re-sending is often where the loop's cost comes from.
Real questions often need facts from several pages. The 2022 Self-Ask paper uses the smallest case, 2 facts from 2 pages: who was president of the United States when superconductivity was discovered? In the paper's figure, GPT-3 answered it with no search at all and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt. That answer is wrong, and one search does no better.
The loop splits the question. Its first search asks when superconductivity was discovered and finds 1911. Its second search, written from that answer, asks who was president in 1911 and finds William Howard Taft.
One search answers from whatever its top result proposes, and the loop writes its second search from what the first one found.
The paper's authors then wrote Bamboogle, 125 questions of this 2-step kind. In the paper's test, Google answered 0.0% of them right from the question as typed. With GPT-3 writing its own follow-up searches, the paper measured 60.0%.1

One search is how **RAG** works in its basic form. Retrieval-augmented generation sends the user's words to a search, puts the top results in the prompt and lets the model answer from them. Ask RAG the superconductivity question, and it answers from whatever ranked first. In agentic search, the model can reject those results and search again.
> 🔗 Retrieval by meaning over your own documents is the subject of **What is Semantic Search?**
> 🔗 Other ways to put a model in the retrieval loop are compared in **Agentic RAG vs CUA vs A2A**
When you build a search agent or debug one that answers wrong, you need to know which part does what. To search, the model writes a request such as `search("Brave Search API price")`: the name of a function your code exposes, and its argument. That request is a tool call. Your code runs the function and sends the result back as the next message.
> 🔗 First time handing a model a function to call? **What is Function Calling?** walks through one call end to end.
Agentic search runs that exchange in a loop, with every decision left to the model: what to search, which page to open and when to answer. The loop has 4 parts:
1.   **The model** writes every query and picks the next move.

2.   **A search tool** sends the query to a search API, which answers from its index: a stored copy of web pages, organized so a query finds the pages that match it.

3.   **A fetch tool** downloads one page the model asks to read in full.

4.   **Your code** starts the run, runs each tool call, sends the result back and stops the run at a cap of 8 model calls.
Your code sends the question and the 2 tools, then runs every tool call and re-sends the whole conversation, until the model answers or your code stops it at 8 calls.
> 🔗 Agents in general? **What is an AI Agent?** covers the loop in which the model decides when to stop.
You choose who does the searching. Build the search and fetch tools yourself, and your code runs every search, so you see each query and set the cap. Or switch on the search a model provider already offers, and its servers do the searching while you write less code.2

You have probably watched this loop without knowing its name. Ask a coding assistant to fix a bug, and it searches your files, reads what it finds and searches again before it answers.
**Coding agents search your code.** Claude Code runs grep and glob, the command-line tools you already use to search file contents and file names, over your repository. Its creator, Boris Cherny, posted in February 2026 that early versions searched a stored index of your files, an approach called RAG. In his words, "we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better." **How Claude Code Actually Works** walks through that search.3
**Deep research usually runs the longest loops.** OpenAI's documentation says its deep research can "find, analyze, and synthesize hundreds of sources", and that a run "can take tens of minutes". Anthropic's own deep research agent is the subject of **How Anthropic Built Multi-Agent Deep Research**.4
**Chat assistants search the web, and ChatGPT moved to the loop in 2026.** David Konitzny measured ChatGPT before and after GPT-5.6 became the default in August 2026. A round is one batch of searches the model sends before it reads any results. In his dataset, 94.0% of prompts got a single round before the change. After the change, 43.5% got one round, and the other 56.5% searched again from what the first round found.5
> ⚠️ **Turning on web search can still mean one search.** OpenAI's documentation describes non-reasoning web search, in which a model that answers without a thinking step sends your question to the search tool and relays the top results.6
A loop that searches again and again can still answer worse than one search. The loop often pays on questions that need more than one page, but only for a model that has learned to run it. The same loop that helps one model can leave another worse off than one search.

Reportedly, two white streetcar conductors had been beaten up after insisting that the soldiers move to the colored section of the cars.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-18) The order was reversed two days later after complaints came from the mayors of cities where the troops were to be moved, including Brownsville, Laredo and Del Rio.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-19)

## April 13, 1911 (Thursday)
[edit]
*   The U.S. House of Representatives passed the bill for a constitutional amendment requiring direct election of U.S. Senators, 296–16.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-60)  
*   Rebels in the Mexican Revolution defeated government troops in an attack on the border city of Agua Prieta, located in Sonora state on the Mexican-U.S. border across from Douglas, Arizona. Stray bullets flew across the border, striking buildings "as far north as Fifteenth Street", and killed two Americans, J.C. Edwards and Robert Harrington.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-62)  
*   British film producer Will Barker carried out his agreement for exhibiting the first motion picture of William Shakespeare's play, _Henry VIII_, after a six-week run in the United Kingdom. Barker had filmed one of the presentations of Sir Herbert Tree's production of the drama, and been allowed to show it to audiences. At Ealing, Barker carried out the burning of all prints of the film.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-63)

[edit]
*   U.S. President Taft sent a warning to the Mexican government and to insurgent leaders to avoid fighting near the border and to not further endanger the lives of Americans.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_May_1911-1)  
*   **Born:**Theodore Romzha, Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church bishop who refused to merge his church with the Russian Orthodox Church; in Nagybocskó, Austria-Hungary (now Velykyi Bychkiv, Ukraine) (murdered, 1944)._[citation needed_]

## April 15, 1911 (Saturday)
[edit]
*   As a followup to an agreement made on June 6, 1909, the $50,000,000 Hukuang loan to China by American, British, French and German Bankers was signed at Beijing.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-64) The Hukuang loan was held up by Russian and Japanese objections, and never made after the revolution in October.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-65)  
*   **Born:**Muhammad Metwally Al Shaarawy, Egyptian Muslim evangelist; in Mit Ghamr (d. 1998)._[citation needed_]

[edit]
*   Elections, supervised by the United States, were held for the National Assembly of Nicaragua. With the assistance of the Army, General Luis Mena, the Minister of War, secured the election of many of his followers to the new legislature.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_May_1911-1)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-66)

## April 17, 1911 (Monday)
[edit]
*   Turning the key in the ignition to start a motor vehicle, rather than having to crank the engine from the outside, became feasible with the filing of the application for the first electric engine starter, by the Dayton Engineering Laboratories Company (DELCO).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-67)Charles F. Kettering of DELCO and Henry M. Leland of the Cadillac Motor Company collaborated with DELCO engineers in developing the system, which would be introduced on Cadillac automobiles in 1912. Kettering would be awarded U.S. Patent No. 1,171,055 on February 8, 1916, under the title "Engine starting, lighting, and ignition system", and DELCO would have exclusive rights to the car starter until 1933._[citation needed_]  
*   The record was set for the highest number of immigrants–11,745—being processed in a single day through the U.S. Bureau of Immigration station at Ellis Island.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-68)  
*   The first public performance of "[Alexander's Ragtime Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander's_Ragtime_Band "Alexander's Ragtime Band")" was given, with the Irving Berlin tune being sung by Emma Carus as part of the Big Easter Vaudeville Carnival at the American Music Hall in Chicago.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-69)  
*   The city of Palm Beach, Florida, was incorporated.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-70)  
*   The Spanish steamer _San Fernando_, on its way from Huelva to Liverpool, sank off of Cape Finisterre. Four people were rescued by the _Portimão_, but 21 others drowned.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-71)

## April 18, 1911 (Tuesday)
[edit]
*   In response to a demand by U.S. President Taft, and the implied threat of an American invasion, Mexico's President Diaz informed Ambassador Wilson that his troops would avoid clashes with rebels near the border shared by the two nations.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-72) The agreement followed the deaths of two Americans in Douglas, Arizona, from fighting in Agua Prieta. Two days later, Diaz's formal note claimed that Americans had aided the rebels and had allowed shots to be fired from the U.S. side of the border.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-73)  
*   **Born:**  
    *   Maurice Goldhaber, Austrian physicist; in Lemberg, Austria-Hungary (now Lviv, Ukraine (d. 2011)._[citation needed_]  
    *   Huntington Hartford, American heir and billionaire, in New York City (d. 2008)._[citation needed_]

*   **Died:** B.V. Matevich-Matsevich, Russian aviator, in a plane crash._[citation needed_]

## April 19, 1911 (Wednesday)
[edit]
Nijinsky
*   Ballet dancers Vaslav Nijinsky and Tamara Karsavina appeared in the first performance of _Le Spectre de la Rose_, choreographed by Michel Fokine. Nijinsky, playing the title role, stunned the audience at the Theatre de Monte Carlo with his exit, soaring into the air on wires and out through an open window.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-74)  
*   Performed for the first time on the very same day was _[Fanny's First Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanny's\_First\_Play "Fanny's First Play")_, at the Adelphi Theatre at Westminster in London. The most successful of George Bernard Shaw's plays, it was introduced anonymously as it lampooned Shaw's critics.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-75)  
*   **Born:**Erich Hartmann, Germany's greatest flying ace who claimed 352 kills in World War II; in Weissach (d. 1993)._[citation needed_]

## April 20, 1911 (Thursday)
[edit]
*   Guarantees of religious freedom and separation of church and state became law in the Republic of Portugal. The new law also ended the centuries-old provision that the Roman Catholic Church was the state religion, and halted government payment of church expenses.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-77)  
*   **Born:**Kukrit Pramoj, Prime Minister of Thailand, 1975 to 1976; in Bangkok (d. 1995)._[citation needed_]

## April 21, 1911 (Friday)
[edit]
*   The U.S. House again passed the Canadian Reciprocity Bill 266–89.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_June_1911-78)  
*   American troops near the Mexican border were ordered to strictly enforce neutrality laws.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_June_1911-78)

## April 22, 1911 (Saturday)
[edit]
*   John J. McNamara, Secretary-Treasurer of the International Association of Structural Iron Workers, was arrested along with two other men and charged with murder for the Los Angeles Times bombing that killed 21 people. His brother James McNamara would escape a death sentence by pleading guilty and would spend the rest of his life in prison, dying 30 years after the October 1 bombing, on March 8, 1941. John McNamara would be released in 1921, two months before his death.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_June_1911-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-79)  
*   The collapse of a railroad bridge at the Cape Colony caused a train to fall into a deep gorge, killing 20 people.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_June_1911-78)  
*   Edwin Blatt, Lawrence Converse and Brown, who had been jailed two months earlier for aiding the rebellion, were released by order of President Diaz.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-AROR_June_1911-78)  
*   Minnesota abolished the death penalty, as Governor Adolph O. Eberhart signed a bill making first degree murder punishable by life in prison.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_1911#cite_note-80)
